items.subject: SCOOP: Looksmaxxer Clavicular Charged With Criminal Rape, Drugging
bullets: Right‑wing livestreamer Braden Peters, known as “Clavicular,” has been charged with criminal rape and drugging according to newly released court documents.
His prior business ties to an Israeli mafia associate have been severed, his alleged overdose occurred five months ago, and his relationship with a powerful publicist has been revived.

Despite the charges, Clavicular’s brand of “looksmaxxing” entered the mainstream (now in Merriam‑Webster) and he recently appeared on Howie Mandel’s podcast, Barstool Sports, Red Scare and the All In show hosted by David Sacks.

items.subject: Trump’s Biggest Con of All
bullets: ProPublica revealed a Russian oligarch funded Donald Trump Jr.'s wedding, which Bettina Trump downplayed as a generous gift without agenda, echoing the family’s typical Russia denial.

The author argues this undisclosed Russia‑Trump link is the most damaging of Trump’s cons, enabling wealth, party corruption, and bolstering Putin’s authoritarian regime while harming the U.S. and the free world.

items.subject: We can’t let Vance’s attacks go unanswered
bullets: Roy Cooper says recent small-dollar donations haven’t met his $200,000 rapid‑response target after Vice President Vance’s rally attacking him and his opponent Michael Whatley.
He warns a new poll shows the North Carolina Senate race virtually tied and that over $100 million from GOP super‑PACs and Trump‑aligned attacks are pressuring his campaign.
Cooper extends the fundraising deadline to 11:59 p.m., urging supporters to chip in to fund air‑wave ads and flip the seat, citing Senate control at stake.

items.subject: Trump’s Gas Price Problem Is About to Get Much, Much Worse (w/ GasBuddy’s Patrick De Haan)
bullets: Escalating Middle East conflict, attacks on Russian refineries, and tight diesel inventories—15% below the five‑year average—are driving oil and diesel prices toward $7‑$8 per gallon this winter.
Refinery utilization is near 98% capacity, leaving little slack for further disruptions as 42 states already see record diesel prices and national gasoline averages rise toward this year’s peak.

items.subject: Trump’s Forever War Is Sucking the Life Out of Him
bullets: Trump’s Iran policy has evolved from a brief engagement to a long‑term, unending conflict, with the author arguing he has no viable exit strategy beyond continued war.
The author predicts that this perpetual war will drain U.S. resources, destabilize regional security, and ultimately lead to Trump’s political downfall.

items.subject: JD Vance just landed in North Carolina
bullets: GOP spending in North Carolina to defeat Roy Cooper has exceeded $100 million, with Trump’s super PAC pouring millions into Michael Whatley’s campaign.
Senate candidate JD Vance is arriving in North Carolina to campaign alongside Whatley, as a new poll shows the race now within the margin of error with six weeks left.
Cooper is launching a $200,000 rapid‑response fund to counter Vance’s attacks and asks supporters to donate immediately.

items.subject: Trump’s AI Hubris Is a Blue Opportunity
bullets: Things are pretty stupid out there, but don’t you ever think they can’t get stupider still. Take the massive Triumphal Arch that our Napoleon-idolizing president wants to build at the entrance to Arlington National Cemetery. The arch, Trump…

Trump’s thinking here, as with his East Wing ballroom, is that the courts will be more deferential in letting him build his arch if he can claim it’s needed for a national security reason. We don’t know whether the appropriate response is t…

items.subject: Trump Threatens to ‘Blow Up’ Iran Again. Not Everyone Thinks He’ll TACO This Time
bullets: Trump, after cutting short a Camp David visit, told Fox he is weighing “wiping Iran out” or a deal and hinted at meeting Iran’s president at the UN, prompting a State Department security alert and Iranian threats to target U.S. bases.

Legal backdrop: New York AG Letitia James sued Trump and his family for business fraud in 2022; they were ordered to pay $450 million in Feb 2024, a verdict upheld in Aug 2025 but the penalty was later thrown out, and Trump is now attempting to prosecute James on dubious charges.

The White House has also banned CNN, MSNBC and Politico, while aides appear unsettled after the departure of press secretary Karoline Leavitt and chief of staff Susie Wiles, raising concerns about Trump’s foreign‑policy moves ahead of the midterms.

items.newsletter: Dan Pfeiffer from The Message Box
items.subject: NBC Poll: The Midterms Are a Referendum on Trump, and He's Losing
bullets: An NBC poll finds Trump’s approval at only low‑40s and a generic Democratic advantage of 5 points, indicating Republicans lack any positive Trump‑driven boost for midterms.
Voters see the midterms as a referendum on Trump, rejecting his agenda and making him a political liability rather than an asset for GOP candidates.

items.subject: Of Donald and Diesel
bullets: Trump demanded Zelensky stop targeting Russian diesel facilities, claiming it hurts U.S. midterm prospects, despite Trump’s own aid cuts leaving Ukraine defenseless.
Krugman argues the global energy crunch is now a refined‑product bottleneck: diesel trades above $200/barrel, driven by refinery outages in the Middle East and Ukraine’s strikes on Russian plants.
Rising diesel costs raise producer prices, feeding core inflation and forcing the Fed to consider higher interest rates, making Trump’s demand politically motivated but unrealistic.

items.subject: The World Is on Fire. Here’s What You Need to Know.
bullets: The Houthis intensified attacks on Saudi Arabia, striking Riyadh, while Ukraine launched a large-scale drone and missile campaign against Moscow and Russian energy sites.
The hosts critique the Trump administration’s handling of the Saudi crisis, assess U.S. involvement in Ukraine, and warn of Russia’s expanding sabotage across Europe and a harsh Ukrainian winter.

items.newsletter: Douglas Macgregor from Warrior Diplomacy Substack
items.subject: America’s Toxic Military Culture Must End
bullets: Macgregor argues that a toxic U.S. military culture, not just presidential decisions, drives endless wars, citing Trump’s Iran conflict as worse than LBJ’s Vietnam escalation.

He warns that even if Democrats win Congress, entrenched Zionist‑backed interests and soaring defense budgets will prevent ending the war, and replacing top officials like SecDef Hegseth won’t fix deep‑rooted Pentagon problems.

items.subject: The One Legit Reason for Dem Panic
bullets: Republican national committees raised about $100 million more than Democrats by July and have pledged $557 million versus Democrats’ $343 million in the nine most competitive Senate races, plus a $13 million cash edge in the House race‑down‑the‑road.

Democratic strategists say GOP’s late‑season ad spending is costly because cheap spring GRP slots are gone, with cost‑per‑GRP jumps of 500% in Anchorage and up to 138% in Michigan, limiting Democratic ad buys despite their candidates out‑raising individual Republican opponents.

The Supreme Court’s ruling lifting limits on coordinated spending lets GOP committees sit on cash and buy low‑rate TV spots in October, prompting Democrats to fear a margin‑cutting ad surge that could shrink their House majority and force intensified fundraising.

items.subject: Robert Kagan’s Chilling Warning About Trump’s Next Two Years | Bulwark on Sunday
bullets: Kagan warns that Trump’s war with Iran is hastening U.S. strategic withdrawal, forcing NATO allies to defend themselves as China and Russia gain operational latitude.
He notes Trump’s lingering ambitions in Greenland and recent Xi Jinping visit to Washington as signs of a chaotic foreign policy lacking coherent direction.
Kagan cautions that the post‑World‑War‑II order could unravel far faster than Washington anticipates, threatening global stability.

items.subject: What a win here could mean
bullets: North Carolina’s Senate race is deemed the pivotal contest that could flip control of the U.S. Senate to Democrats, giving them 51 votes.
Republican opponents have spent over $100 million on the race, and a new brand‑new poll shows the contest within the margin of error.
Cooper urges donors to contribute $5 to help secure a Democratic win and advance policies on health care, voting rights, and tax relief for working families.

items.subject: Kash Patel’s Eyebrow Has Gone Rogue | The Trio
bullets: The Trio dissect Milo Yiannopoulos' chaotic divorce, a GOP nominee's connections to the Unite the Right rally, Victor Marx's campaign scandals, and a candidate duped by a fake Kai Trump account.
They analyze Kash Patel's contentious congressional hearing and criticize his eyebrow‑raising request for $1.5 billion in FBI funding.
The episode also features a Republican congressional candidate who released a 20‑song rap album praising Trump.

items.subject: Can Democrat Troy Jackson Oust Republican Senator Susan Collins in Maine?
bullets: Democratic nominee Troy Jackson, with just seven weeks left, faces incumbent Republican Susan Collins in a race that recent polls show as dead‑locked after Graham Platner’s withdrawal","Jackson frames the contest as a ‘change election’, attacking Collins on her anti‑abortion record, high gas prices and opposing Medicare for All, while fielding questions about Joe Manchin’s endorsement and his own past Republican ties
The full 20‑minute live Substack interview is available to paid subscribers, with a one‑minute preview for free users

items.subject: RFK Jr.’s ‘Medical Freedom’ Comes With a Body Count
bullets: On September 11, an unvaccinated individual with measles spent nearly seven hours at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, including time in the cafeteria, atrium, and NICU lounge, potentially exposing hundreds of patients and staff to the virus.

Philadelphia Deputy Health Commissioner James Garrow confirmed the measles exposure, highlighting the heightened risk to NICU infants who lack maternal antibodies and are especially vulnerable to infection.
The incident underscores criticism of RFK Jr.’s anti‑vaccine stance and calls for stronger public health response as he assumes the role of Health and Human Services secretary.

items.subject: Why Does Everyone Hate Trump’s Tariffs?
bullets: Trump’s April 2025 tariffs (10‑48%) failed to boost U.S. manufacturing jobs or construction spending and pushed import prices higher, contrary to admin predictions.

Despite the tariffs, neither a U.S. nor global recession materialized, retaliation was limited, and countries like India and the EU advanced free‑trade deals, while domestic political support stayed around 20% and was confined to Trump loyalists.

items.subject: Anne Applebaum: Putin Played Jared Kushner “Like a Fiddle”
bullets: Applebaum argues Putin manipulated Jared Kushner, treating him as a pliable instrument in Russia’s geopolitical games.

Miller claims the Trump administration is deploying tech entrepreneurs and hedge‑funders to run a covert influence operation in Greenland while simultaneously seizing Venezuelan gold and oil and backing the Bolsonaro family in Brazil, possibly linked to Elon Musk’s grievances.
The episode also promotes Applebaum’s Atlantic cover story “Empire of Grift,” her novel recommendation “Whistler,” and announces a Bulwark benefit event in Springfield, Ohio.

items.subject: Alex Wagner NUKES Alito’s Defense of the Trump Election Power Grab
bullets: Alex Wagner and JVL map how four conservative operatives constructed a legal infrastructure that remade the Supreme Court over decades and underpins today’s partisan politics.
They dissect Justice Samuel Alito’s dissent in the Supreme Court’s mail‑ballot decision, arguing it shields Trump’s ongoing battle over the Kennedy Center’s leadership.
The Bulwark’s Good Fight Tour will hit Columbia, Charlotte (with Pete Buttigieg) and Atlanta Oct 16‑18; tickets are on TheBulwark.com/Events.

items.subject: This Week in Palestine: Gaza Building Collapse Kills 12 Kids, as Trump Plans to Send Israel 2,000-Pound Bombs
bullets: A war‑damaged building collapsed in Gaza City, killing 12 children and 9 adults; rescue workers used bare hands amid Israel’s restrictions on heavy machinery, saving dozens of trapped residents.

Israel’s continued airstrikes in Gaza killed a 15‑year‑old boy, while settler violence in the West Bank escalated; a leading Israeli think tank warned that “Jewish terrorism” poses a strategic threat to Israel.

items.subject: Almost six weeks until Election Day
bullets: The North Carolina Democratic Party’s coordinated campaign knocked on 37,000 doors and made 25,000 calls last weekend, reaching over 60,000 voters in a single week.
Nearly 15,000 volunteers have been active statewide, and the campaign urges continued weekend canvassing, phone banking, and personal outreach to maintain momentum for the 45 days until Election Day.

items.subject: Noura Erakat On Why She Was Arrested for Protesting Israeli Bond Investments
bullets: Lydia Ghuman of the Internationalist Law Center says Florida is a test case for Zionist influence, noting Israel is the only foreign nation receiving such large local taxpayer bond investments

items.subject: “I liked imagining us listening to the same song at the same time. It was the only piece of connection I had left.”
bullets: After a 2023 divorce, stepmother Chloé Caldwell kept a bond with her 13‑year‑old stepdaughter by continuously adding songs to a shared playlist, eventually reuniting at her father’s 2025 memorial where they played “Blackbird” together.

AI safety researcher Joe Benton quit Anthropic’s safety team to join independent evaluator METR, warning that AI agents could soon surpass human intelligence, with recent hacks and social‑engineering incidents suggesting industry under‑investment in safety could threaten humanity’s survival.

MrBeast (Jimmy Donaldson) has built a billion‑dollar empire, amassing over 500 million YouTube subscribers (≈6% of world population) and a record‑breaking Amazon reality show, while monetizing extreme stunts and philanthropy that often involve personal hardship for content.

items.subject: Focus Groups Are Revealing a HUGE Weakness for Republicans
bullets: Sarah Longwell’s focus groups in San Francisco show Republicans lack a clear, relatable narrative on everyday issues, making them vulnerable to voter disengagement.
She argues the GOP’s messaging fails to address middle‑class concerns, with respondents citing confusion over policy priorities and distrust of party leaders.

items.newsletter: Dan Pfeiffer from The Message Box
items.subject: What the Hell Was Gavin Newsom Thinking?
bullets: Newsom told Jake Tapper he wouldn’t run for president if Kamala Harris entered the race, sparking criticism that he’s limiting his own prospects just 50 days before the election.
Pfeiffer argues the comment is a tactical move to avoid a contentious primary with Harris, whose national popularity may rival Newsom’s, and notes the backlash on social media and among subscribers.

items.subject: MAGA’s Alternate Realities, Fractured Elbows, and a Fast-Moving War
bullets: George Conway, Andrew Egger and Catherine Rampell appeared on an emergency Kennedy Center livestream discussing the rapid escalation of the Iran‑Israel war and why Washington is struggling to keep pace.

Sarah Longwell’s new bestseller, highlighted with an excerpt and a book‑tour stop in Dayton, Ohio, uses a personal “fractured elbow” metaphor to argue for a principled, bipartisan approach to politics.
The newsletter memorializes late Arizona Sen. Jon Kyl, crediting his “Kyl Style” of direct, truth‑telling debate as a model for current conservative discourse.

items.subject: Economic Size and Economic Power
bullets: Krugman argues that in weaponized interdependence, the welfare loss from cutting off imports (consumer surplus) usually exceeds the loss to exporters because import demand is less elastic than export supply.
He cites the Canada‑U.S. trade dispute over Alberta tar sands oil as a case where export‑side producer surplus is significant, warning that policymakers often underestimate such export losses.

items.subject: This Week in Democracy – Week 87: Trump Bans CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from White House and Lashes Out at Supreme …
bullets: The Supreme Court rejected Trump’s attempt to restrict mail‑in voting, a rare Democratic win, but the ruling was cryptic and is expected to spark further legal battles through 2028.

Trump fired back at his own Court nominees, threatened to tear down the Kennedy Center if he can’t name it, and banned CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House for negative coverage, citing First Amendment violations.

items.subject: Abdul El-Sayed Hits Back Against His Critics
bullets: In a candid interview, Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El‑Sayed calls Vice President JD Vance “idiot ass boss,” labels Trump “vain” and “narcissistic,” and brands GOP rival Mike Rogers a “coward” who skipped their debate.

El‑Sayed condemns Trump’s $2.8 billion weapons package for Israel as ineffective, criticizes billionaire Robert Kraft’s pressure on Macklemore’s tour, and decries media focus on Hasan Piker and attacks on his wife’s medical practice.
Subscribers can watch the full half‑hour video interview; free users get a two‑minute preview, with an upgrade link provided to bypass the Zeteo paywall.

items.subject: The gap is closing. Fast.
bullets: A new poll shows NC Senate race between Roy Cooper and GOP’s Michael Whatley is now within the margin of error, with Whatley closing in on the lead.
Trump, Stephen Miller, and super PACs are spending over $100 million on ads against Cooper, aiming to keep Senate control for the GOP through 2029.
Cooper urges immediate grassroots donations, asking supporters to give $5 to counter the GOP’s spending advantage.

items.subject: We’re Living in an Insane Asylum
bullets: President Biden accused the Democratic Party of plotting to assassinate him, a claim the hosts say is being ignored while diesel prices surge dramatically.
The show riffs on Trump’s wish to demolish the Kennedy Center, Joe Manchin’s posthumous‑style endorsement of Susan Collins, and a 90% odds estimate that AI won’t wipe out humanity.
Sarah’s book How to Eat an Elephant hit #2 on the NYT bestseller list, and the hosts promote a Bulwark LIVE tour in October with guests like Bakari Sellers, Pete Buttigieg, and Bill Kristol.

items.subject: From ‘The Odyssey’ to ‘Spider-Man,’ a Summer for Everyone
bullets: Christopher Nolan’s three‑hour “The Odyssey” has earned nearly $1.7 billion worldwide, topping daily box‑office charts with over $1 million per day through mid‑September and reviving interest in the classic epic.

Spider‑Man: Brand New Day became the highest‑grossing domestic film after 47 days, proving superhero movies remain box‑office powerhouses, and its writer Chris McKenna discussed story choices and upcoming Avengers projects.

Zach Cregger’s “Resident Evil” is positioned as an awards contender, deliberately mimicking video‑game mechanics with relentless action sequences, while a Donnie Darko anniversary screening returns to theaters Oct 2‑4.

items.subject: Canada’s Break With Trump Just Got MUCH Bigger
bullets: Mark Carney’s soaring popularity fuels Canada’s pivot toward the EU and a new defense posture as U.S. ties fray under Trump’s inflation‑driven policies.
Trump’s record shows rising inflation and pressure on the Fed, while former governor Kevin Warsh employs a covert strategy to shield Fed independence.
IRS data reveal a massive tax gap and billions wasted on idle federal workers, highlighting how disappearing government data erodes accountability.

items.subject: John Barnett gave his life exposing Boeing. A new film spotlights his fight.
bullets: John Barnett, a Boeing quality manager for 32 years, warned of missing parts, debris, and pressure to bypass procedures before his 2024 suicide, which a coroner ruled self‑inflicted.
A Senate investigation in 2024 heard from over a dozen Boeing whistleblowers, including Sam Mohawk and Sam Salehpour, who reported similar safety concerns and retaliation, echoing Barnett’s claims.

Boeing settled Barnett’s mother’s wrongful‑death suit for at least $50,000 and undisclosed terms on the retaliation claim, without admitting liability, while whistleblower documents continued to expose systemic manufacturing problems.

items.subject: It’s Zohran vs. Trump on Immigration
bullets: New York City and 21 other states sued the Trump administration for rescinding the 2022 public‑charge rule, arguing the new vague policy violates the Administrative Procedure Act and expands discretionary denials of visas and green cards for anyone using public benefits such as Medicaid, SNAP, and housing assistance.

The lawsuit claims the change will force up to 4 million people—including 1.8 million children—to drop out of health and welfare programs, potentially raising premature death rates in immigrant communities by 10.6 % and costing New York City billions in emergency care.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: Why Do We Even Have a Constitution Day?
bullets: Trump’s White House is simultaneously pushing a sweeping sanctions package targeting Russia’s elite and energy sector while also discussing pre‑war business deals with Russia, revealing a contradictory policy stance on Ukraine and Russia.

The author argues that Constitution Day is under‑celebrated because July 4, commemorating the Declaration of Independence, is seen as more foundational, yet the Constitution’s enduring relevance demands renewed liberal constitutionalism to defend democracy amid unprecedented attacks.

items.subject: Expiring at Midnight: Bonus for New Upgrades
bullets: Doomberg offers a midnight‑deadline bonus giving subscribers full access to a deep‑dive presentation on Chevron, the energy supermajor, plus all new full‑length articles and its 500‑plus‑article archive.

The promotion builds on their Dec 2023 piece arguing that unifying Western Hemisphere energy production could neutralize Middle‑East oil influence, positioning the analysis as a key geopolitical insight.

items.subject: The Kennedy Center Lost $30 Million in Pledges and Wrote Off $48 Million in ‘Bad Debt’ Amid Trump’s Takeover
bullets: The Kennedy Center’s 2025 tax return shows $48 million in bad‑debt expense and a $30 million drop in pledges and grants after Trump’s takeover, leaving it reliant on $257 million in congressional appropriations to avoid a deficit.
Despite Trump’s claim of “hundreds of millions” in losses, the Center reported $517 million in revenue and $210 million in net revenue, with record $778 million net assets as of Sept. 30, 2025.
A federal judge barred adding Trump’s name to the Center’s exterior, prompting the administration to close the venue, while ticket sales and donations fell further after the naming attempt.

items.subject: Fear Strikes Out
bullets: Ursula von der Leyen announced a symbolic EU‑Canada “associate member” plan, backed by Prime Minister Mark Carney, prompting Trump’s angry threat to cut EU trade, which was largely ignored.

Krugman argues that global fear of Trump has evaporated as the US has faltered militarily in Iran and economically in trade disputes, leaving Trump hated but not feared, contrary to Machiavelli’s advice.

Despite Canada’s heavy US trade dependence and geographic disadvantage, Canadian leaders are pushing the EU pivot, reflecting a broader international belief that Trump lacks the power to punish dissent after recent setbacks.

items.subject: Two days left to comment on HHS's vaccine category proposal
bullets: HHS issued a short‑notice (30‑day) Request for Information to reconsider vaccine recommendation categories, potentially shifting routine shots to “shared clinical decision‑making” and weakening ACIP linkage, which could cause confusion and jeopardize insurance coverage.

The proposal follows Executive Order 14420 aiming to cut the childhood schedule from 18 to 11 diseases and promote single‑antigen MMR, and a prior attempt to reclassify several vaccines was blocked by a federal judge.
Comments are due by September 20, 2026 (docket HHS‑OS‑2026‑0332) and the public is urged to submit input to counter a docket that may be skewed toward narrowing vaccine access.

items.subject: Coming to America
bullets: The Houthis’ rapid advance along the Red Sea coast has damaged Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline and intensified a looming global diesel shortage after weeks of Hormuz disruptions, pushing the economy toward a crisis.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s reliance on U.S. military support appears weakened, raising the risk that internal and external foes could topple the regime and trigger a ‘full‑tilt’ shock to global markets.

Chinese refiners have surged back into crude purchases, driving Shanghai yuan‑denominated oil futures to a 2018‑high of 929.4 yuan ($138.50) per barrel, positioning China to profit from the Middle East turmoil as President Xi prepares a Washington visit.

items.subject: Trump, Putin, and the Ongoing Plot to Undermine Our Elections
bullets: David Corn’s new book “How Russia Won” argues that Russia will likely target the 2026 midterms with disinformation supporting Trump’s election‑rigging claims, while U.S. agencies stay silent.

Corn claims Democrats mishandled the 2016 Trump‑Russia scandal, labeling Trump’s alignment with a foreign adversary as a betrayal even if not illegal, and warns Michael Cohen may be re‑aligning with Trump.

items.subject: Wanna Influence Sean Duffy? Try His Son-in-Law’s Campaign.
bullets: Covenant Logistics CEO David Parker donated $10,000 to Wisconsin candidate Michael Alfonso, the son‑in‑law of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, despite no ties to the state.

Alfonso’s campaign received additional support from other transportation‑industry donors who have business before the DOT, which recently renewed a two‑year exemption for Covenant’s driver‑training rules for five more years.

items.subject: ‘Were You Drunk?’ Mehdi Confronts Islamophobic GOP Congresswoman Nancy Mace in Heated Piers Morgan Debate
bullets: Nancy Mace called every Muslim officeholder a “trojan horse” and claimed “all terrorists are Muslims,” prompting Mehdi to confront her on Piers Uncensored, accusing her of Islamophobia and blind support for Israel and Trump.

During the heated exchange, Mace repeatedly interrupted and alleged Mehdi was “jihad adjacent,” while Mehdi presented staff testimonies that Mace allegedly sent aides to buy alcohol at odd hours, which she denies.

items.subject: EXCLUSIVE: Inside the Democratic Party’s Trump Oversight Plans
bullets: Vice President JD Vance downplayed Watergate, saying a modern scandal would get only half a day’s news, implying the Trump administration is eclipsing Nixon’s norm‑breaking legacy.
Young MAGA conservatives are producing hype videos and nostalgic content glorifying Nixon, mirroring their admiration for Trump’s defiance of institutional norms.
Democrats cite the post‑Nixon investigations into government corruption as a blueprint for new oversight measures targeting alleged Trump‑era misconduct.

items.subject: Canada Is Making America Its B*tch
bullets: Canada is shifting from a close ally to a strategic competitor, positioning itself as a counterweight to U.S. influence in foreign affairs and the bond market, according to the newsletter’s analysis.

items.subject: The president’s rally in NC just changed everything
bullets: President’s overnight rally in North Carolina boosted GOP super‑PAC spending, pushing dark‑money attacks over $100 million and threatening to erase Roy Cooper’s slight polling edge against Michael Whatley.
The campaign now needs an additional $38,000 by 11:59 p.m. tonight to fund new TV ads and voter outreach, aiming to reverse the momentum and flip the Senate seat blue for the first time since 2008.

items.subject: Hasan Piker Says America Has Killed Lots of People. Donald Trump Agrees
bullets: Hasan Piker told Axios that, pound for pound, the U.S. has caused more deaths than al‑Qaeda, citing 432,000 civilian deaths in Iraq, Afghanistan, Syria, Yemen and Pakistan (2001‑2023) and over 300,000 in Vietnam, 150,000 in Laos and up to 1 million in Indonesia’s anti‑Communist massacres.

Piker highlighted U.S. airstrikes on a school in Minab that killed 150 people, including more than 100 children, as an example of American terror under Trump’s administration, arguing that such killings are “acts of terror.”

The Axios clip, released as a 56‑second preview, sparked backlash from right‑wing commentator Scott Jennings, liberal activist Shannon Watts, and Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El‑Sayed, who distanced himself from Piker’s remarks.

items.subject: Ben Shapiro’s New Anti-Muslim Movie Is Truly Bad
bullets: The author condemns Ben Shapiro’s anti‑Muslim action thriller ‘Run Hide Fight: Infidels’, calling it poorly made and full of offensive stereotypes, such as a terrorist kicking a gay ally and an Asian‑American student defusing bombs solely because he’s Asian.
He highlights the film’s reliance on hateful tropes and its low‑budget, shoddy execution, arguing it does more damage to conservative credibility than any political message.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: Congress to Trump: MORE TARIFFS, PLEASE!
bullets: The House passed a bipartisan Russia sanctions bill that, besides punishing Russian leadership and industries, gives Trump discretionary authority to impose up to 100% tariffs on top importers of Russian energy, a concession meant to win his support for Ukraine aid.

Critics note the tariff powers are a dangerous expansion of Trump’s trade war toolkit, ignoring his history of using narrow tariff authorities for broad protectionist aims, and more than a dozen GOP members tried unsuccessfully to strip the provisions before the vote.
The bill cleared the Senate 86‑0 and the House 262‑? despite concerns from Democrats like Hakeem Jeffries and some Republicans that the tariff provisions outweigh the sanctions’ benefits.

items.subject: EXCLUSIVE: Biden’s Genocide Accomplices Targeted by New Accountability Campaign
bullets: A coalition of human‑rights groups launched the #DropTheGenocide20 pledge, urging employers not to hire 20 top Biden‑Harris officials they say promoted, lied about, or covered up the Gaza genocide.
The campaign targets former Biden officials now in academia, think tanks and media, demanding they be barred from future Democratic administrations for their alleged role in the conflict.

items.subject: Fuels and our Money
bullets: Krugman highlights that U.S. gasoline pump prices have risen sharply over the past year, equating the increase to a higher dollars‑per‑barrel cost for 42‑gallon gallons.
He notes the global economy has shown surprising resilience despite these fuel cost spikes, but warns that there may be limits to this durability.

items.subject: Watch Me Live (Or probably not)
bullets: The European Central Bank’s 11th Annual Research Conference on 16 June 2026 will feature speeches on monetary policy, inflation dynamics, and the eurozone’s post‑pandemic recovery.
Key speakers include ECB policymakers, leading academics, and industry experts who will present new research on fiscal‑monetary coordination and climate‑related financial risks.
The event will be streamed online, but live attendance may be limited due to ongoing health restrictions.

items.subject: Here’s Who Trump Should Blame for the Rate Hike He’s Raging About
bullets: The Fed raised rates again, citing persistent inflation and geopolitical risks, and most officials now expect at least one more hike before year‑end.

Trump blames the Fed for higher rates, but the article argues his tariffs, Iran war escalation, and inflated consumer price expectations—up to 4.6% annual—have driven the inflation the Fed must combat.
A new Receipts With Catherine Rampell podcast launches September 18, covering these economic and political dynamics.

items.subject: ‘60 Minutes’ Is Now 'Dead' and Bari'd
bullets: CBS staffers say the Bari Weiss‑overhauled ‘60 Minutes’ debut drew only 7.9 million viewers (1.6 million 25‑54 demo), a 21% total and 33% demo drop from last season’s 10.03 million/2.36 million launch
They warn the ratings disaster signals broader damage to CBS (‘the Tiffany Network’) under Weiss’s changes, calling the new format a mismatched Frankenstein

items.subject: Palestinian Ambassador Says UK Government Told Him Tougher Restrictions on UK Arms to Israel Are Coming

The interview traces Vance’s shift from a Yale‑law‑school Trump critic to a MAGA figure, questioning whether his reversal was inevitable or sparked by specific influences.

The newsletter urges subscribers to upgrade to a Zeteo UK content bundle or gift subscriptions, positioning the event as a milestone in the brand’s global expansion.

items.subject: Impeach Them. All of Them.

Thomas Massie introduced eight impeachment articles against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of war‑making violations in Iran and Yemen, civilian‑casualty negligence, extrajudicial killings in the Caribbean/Eastern Pacific, retaliation against Sen. Mark Kelly, and an illegal kidnapping plot against Nicolás Maduro.

bullets: ICE set a new August record with 50,925 arrests, targeting non‑criminal immigrants such as spouses of citizens, legal asylum seekers, and former TPS holders like Haitians.

The Trump administration redirected funds from SNAP and Medicaid to ICE, coupled with dehumanizing rhetoric and illegal deportations, creating a bureaucratic cruelty that masks indifference to human dignity.

items.subject: Less than one month until early voting
bullets: Less than 29 days until early voting in North Carolina, with 48 days until Election Day, the campaign is intensifying GOTV efforts through door‑knocking, calls, and community visits to secure votes for the blue seat.
Voters can locate early voting sites and hours via the provided link, and those not registered can do so on the same day they vote; the newsletter urges a $5 contribution to sustain outreach.
National Voter Registration Day is highlighted, offering links to register, learn how, and mail in registration forms for those who need to sign up before the early voting period.

items.subject: Robotics Tipping Point: A Citrini Field Trip
bullets: Robotics is at a tipping point: basic humanoid locomotion is now cheap and reliable, while dexterous manipulation is advancing through multiple hardware approaches, enabling near‑term commercial use like package sorting.

Recent demos such as GeneralistAI’s GEN‑1.5 one‑shot learner, Skild AI’s pancake‑flipping robot, and China’s World Robotics Games show early generalization but still lack high utility, suggesting the “ChatGPT moment” will be a gradual mosaic of breakthroughs rather than a single event.
Investors should watch for integrated systems that combine locomotion, dexterity, and autonomy—these are emerging faster than expected and could drive the next wave of AI‑enabled physical products.

bullets: Rep. Thomas Massie filed a privileged House resolution introducing eight impeachment articles against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of illegal wars in Iran and Yemen, extrajudicial killings, and civilian‑casualty violations, forcing a floor vote tomorrow unless Speaker Johnson recesses the chamber

Bill Kristol argues that despite Trump’s 13‑point win in Iowa and larger margins in other Great Plains states, shifting public opinion on tariffs, war, and candidate quality makes Democratic Senate and gubernatorial races in Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, South Dakota, and Texas surprisingly competitive, with several polls showing Democrats or independents within a few points of incumbents

Andrew Egger reports the Future of Life Institute’s Pro‑Human Assembly highlighted growing bipartisan alarm over uncontrolled AI‑driven robots, but notes the lack of a coordinated political strategy to address the existential risk

items.newsletter: Here Be Dragons from Barbara F. Walter
items.subject: Ukraine Changed How I Think About Civil War
bullets: Ukraine’s use of cheap drones, AI, and satellite‑linked software shows that small, tech‑savvy forces can out‑innovate larger militaries, but the author warns that governments can eventually counter‑act with massive surveillance, data integration, and scalable autonomous weapons.

In a civil conflict, the state’s advantages—vast funding, manufacturing, AI‑driven facial‑recognition and communications control—could enable it to locate and eliminate rebels, shifting the long‑term power balance back to the regime despite early underdog advantages.

The author concludes that while emerging tech may initially empower citizens against external foes, the same technologies could make internal authoritarian control far more lethal, potentially leaving both sides worse off.

items.subject: Two Democrats Walk Into Fox News
bullets: Pete Buttigieg discusses the value of productive disagreement with Fox News co-host Jessica Tarlov, emphasizing that engaging with opposing views is essential for meaningful politics in an ideologically siloed era.
Tarlov, a daily Fox host surrounded by conservative co‑hosts, has published a book detailing lessons learned from engaging the other side, illustrating her efforts to broaden viewers’ perspectives.

items.subject: Wave goodbye
bullets: Ossoff urges supporters to donate $10 to his 2026 Georgia Senate reelection, arguing the seat is critical for Democrats to regain Senate control and stop MAGA policies
He recalls flipping the Georgia Senate seat in 2020 against pundit expectations, framing the upcoming midterms as the last chance to restore checks and balances

items.subject: Don’t Think Trump Won’t Demolish the Kennedy Center – He’s Shown Us Who He Is
bullets: Trump is threatening to rename or demolish the Kennedy Center because he cannot attach his own name to the historic venue, reflecting his pattern of personalizing institutions.
The newsletter cites the 2018 Kavanaugh sexual assault allegation as an example of Trump’s allies surviving scandals while the judiciary shifts far right, linking it to his current cultural attacks.

It also notes rapper Macklemore’s silencing for pro‑Palestine remarks, Ed Sheeran’s refusal to support him, and the resulting fallout for Sheeran’s tour, illustrating broader cultural backlash against perceived cowardice.

items.subject: What AI can and cannot do in biosecurity
bullets: AI accelerates biological knowledge (e.g., protein folding, gene‑editing, literature synthesis) but still requires wet‑lab work, so the barrier to creating dangerous pathogens remains largely physical.

Anthropic documented five cases where its Claude model helped design more transmissible viruses or more potent toxins, prompting bans and tighter safeguards, illustrating both misuse potential and current limits.

Experts argue AI marginally raises biosecurity risk, urging urgent actions: protect sensitive data, increase transparency of AI‑bio research, and de‑escalate geopolitical AI races to ensure benefits outweigh threats.

items.subject: Conferencing, Day 1
bullets: At an ECB conference on geoeconomics, Steve Redding (with Liu, Yang, and Smith‑Worthington) presented a model showing US power now hinges significantly on the strength of its alliances, measured by how domestic interest changes affect actions globally.
The papers discussed were highly technical—eigenvectors and trading equilibria—but offered a potential framework for translating complex models into current policy analysis.

items.subject: Value Trap
bullets: In July 2025 Angola cut diesel subsidies by a third, sparking three days of violent protests that left 30 dead, 277 injured and 1,500 arrested before the government kept the higher prices.

The Permian Basin now produces over 23 bcf/d of dry gas, far exceeding local demand and allowing producers to give away fuel, while Alberta consumes about 7 bcf/d of its 11 bcf/d output, leaving only 4 bcf/d for export and creating a political dilemma for Premier Danielle Smith amid a separatist referendum and trade tensions.

Smith’s cabinet leak revealed internal debates on how to expand Alberta’s cheap natural‑gas sales to data‑center builders without alienating voters who rely on the domestic supply, highlighting the broader challenge of balancing local subsidies with export ambitions.

items.subject: Thomas Massie Has a Nasty Surprise for Pete Hegseth
bullets: Thomas Massie filed articles of impeachment against conservative commentator Pete Hegseth, accusing him of inciting violence and spreading falsehoods.

The hosts note that Gov. Gavin Newsom appears to be stepping back from a presidential bid, and they call out a notoriously racist Republican candidate running for Texas railroad commissioner.

items.subject: Big AI Wants You to Believe It Could Destroy the World – So It Can Fill Its Pockets
bullets: Nate Soares argues that AI researchers warn of a real existential threat within a decade, citing self‑improving models from OpenAI and Anthropic that could surpass human control and potentially annihilate humanity.

Paris Marx counters that the “end‑of‑humanity” warnings are sensationalist, noting that current AI systems still require human oversight and that claims of imminent superintelligence lack concrete evidence.

The newsletter highlights a recent thread by former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon claiming a race toward autonomous superintelligence, but stresses the need for caution before accepting such dramatic predictions.

items.subject: EXCLUSIVE: The Next Big Dem Proposal: Let Kids Eat Free
bullets: Searchlight Institute proposes a national plan to give every public school child free breakfast and lunch, costing a few billion dollars a year and expanding the current program that only serves the poorest families.

The proposal argues that universal free meals reduce stigma, lower administrative costs, and invest in children’s future, citing the pandemic‑era federal subsidy that temporarily covered all school meals.

Current federal school lunch program serves 29 million kids daily, with 21 million receiving free or discounted meals, yet many eligible families miss out due to complex enrollment and lack of awareness.

items.subject: Even George Conway Wasn’t Ready for Kash Patel’s Senate Hearing
bullets: Trump lashes out at the Supreme Court after his appointees helped block his administration’s mail‑ballot rules, prompting George Conway and Sam Stein to debate the ruling and its midterm implications.
In a Senate hearing, Kash Patel attempts to explain a bizarre FBI controversy involving alleged mishandling of evidence, which Conway describes as one of the strangest and grossest cases ever heard.
The Bulwark is hosting a benefit live event in Dayton, Ohio on September 25, with proceeds supporting the Haitian Community Help and Support Center in Springfield.

items.subject: Meet the British TV Host Who Says She Was Taken Off Air Over Gaza
bullets: Long‑time ITV daytime host Nadia Sawalha says she was abruptly removed from ‘Loose Women’ after publicly supporting Palestine following the Oct 7 Gaza war, with producers citing ‘noise’.

Sawalha has filed legal action against ITV, hoping the case will set a precedent against unfair treatment of individuals expressing moral convictions, and discusses related libel damages from the Daily Mail.
The inaugural ‘Sangita Meets…’ podcast interview, available to paid Zeteo subscribers, covers her Jordanian heritage, accusations of antisemitism, and the potential career impact of suing ITV.

items.subject: AI CEOs Would Very Much Like Congress to Save the World
bullets: A whistleblower warned AI firms’ products pose a >10% chance of human extinction, prompting CEOs of Anthropic, OpenAI and xAI to demand congressional guardrails, which the author suggests may be a move toward regulatory capture.
Senators Alex Padilla, Chris Murphy and others express concern that AI CEOs are hiring former lawmakers and funding anti‑state regulation efforts, while noting China’s role in amplifying AI fears.

The piece highlights divergent views: Bernie Sanders trusts CEOs’ expertise, whereas critics cite Elon Musk’s deceptive history and Sam Altman’s alleged sociopathy, leaving the legislative outcome uncertain.

items.subject: The Brand New NYT Poll Is a Disaster for Republicans
bullets: The New York Times/Siena poll shows Democrats leading likely voters for Congress by nearly 9 points, matching the 2018 margin that helped them gain 40 House seats.
The lead is driven by Trump’s unpopularity, economic dissatisfaction, and widespread disapproval of his handling of issues, especially the cost of living.
The poll also reveals deeper GOP challenges that contradict conventional wisdom, threatening Republican majorities beyond the generic ballot advantage.

items.subject: Democrats Should Demagogue AI. Seriously.
bullets: The author argues Democrats should weaponize AI-driven demagoguery to win elections by appealing to conspiracy‑mindset voters who have gravitated toward the GOP.
He claims this strategy uniquely combines decent policy, a popular movement, and a chance to outflank Republicans now tainted by Trump’s alignment with oligarchs.

items.subject: Ed Sheeran Isn’t Staying Out of Politics – He Is Letting a Pro-Israel Billionaire Choose His Politics for Him
bullets: Macklemore performed a pro‑Palestinian song at Ed Sheeran’s MetLife Stadium show, after which he was abruptly removed from the rest of the U.S. tour.
Sheeran has remained silent about the incident, which the author argues is not neutrality but a tacit endorsement of billionaire Robert Kraft’s pro‑Israel influence over his tour politics.
The piece suggests Kraft’s financial power is shaping the political messaging of high‑profile artists like Sheeran, effectively sidelining dissenting voices such as Macklemore’s.

items.subject: The Week’s Pressure Systems: Toxic Air, a $5,000 Promise, and a Map That Finally Tells the Truth
bullets: Donald Trump pledged a $5,000 “Trump dividend” to every adult if Republicans keep Congress, but the $1.2 trillion cost far exceeds current tariff revenue and lacks any authorized funding.

items.subject: AI Is an Existential Political Threat to the GOP
bullets: Top AI researchers, including Anthropic’s Jacob Coxon and CEO Dario Amodei, warned that frontier AI could create a dangerous internet‑taking botnet within 6‑12 months, prompting alarm from Elon Musk and Sam Altman.

items.subject: Why Is Trump Still Boosting AI?

The AI boom, once a political asset for Trump, is becoming a liability as public backlash grows and the promised productivity gains remain unproven.

items.subject: Will Dems Help ‘Supercharge’ Trump’s Crypto Corruption?

items.subject: Respiratory increasing, while Covid-19 peaking? Also, the air after 9/11 killed more than the actual attack
bullets: ILI reports show a rise in common cold cases and a possible Covid‑19 peak, with wastewater levels dropping in the South, Midwest and Northeast but still climbing in the West.

U.S. measles cases have surged to ~3,300 in 2026, driven by outbreaks in Pennsylvania (676 cases, 3 deaths), Ohio (133) and Wisconsin (over 160), underscoring the need for vaccination in affected areas.

The World Trade Center Health Program, covering over 104,000 responders and survivors, finds that half of participants have certified health conditions—1 in 8 cancer and 1 in 5 non‑cancer—highlighting long‑term disaster health impacts.

items.subject: Yesterday’s rally in Athens
bullets: Ossoff rallied a large Athens crowd, urging voters to turn out in a month to defeat Trump‑aligned Rep. Mike Collins and elect Democratic candidates, including Gov. Bottoms for Medicaid expansion.
He accused Trump of inflating prices, mismanaging wars, and funneling $620 million Pentagon loans to his son’s venture, while calling for a constitutional amendment to overturn Citizens United.

items.subject: How to Stop AI From Killing Humanity
bullets: Nate Soares argues that any development of smarter‑than‑human AI using current methods carries a high probability of human extinction, estimating at least a 10% chance if rushed.
He notes a growing wave of AI researchers and company employees publicly warning that the race toward superintelligence could kill all humans within a decade.
Soares questions why leading AI firms, despite these alarms, are not halting development, implying corporate incentives outweigh existential risk concerns.

items.subject: The Latest Right-Wing Revolt Against Markwayne Mullin Is the Wildest Yet
bullets: Conservative pundits, from Benny Johnson to Tomi Lahren, are enraged that DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin gave no concrete plan to deport Rep. Ilhan Omar, a claim based on a dubious anonymous forum post.

Despite repeated MAGA promises and a Justice Department claim of an immigration‑fraud probe, no credible evidence supports the allegation Omar married her brother, yet right‑wing influencers continue to demand her deportation.

Mullin’s silence has sparked a backlash across Fox News, The Blaze, and pro‑Trump influencers, who accuse him of protecting Omar and threaten to hold him accountable for unfulfilled mass‑deportation promises.

items.subject: BOMBSHELL: Russian Oligarch Bankrolled Don Jr.’s Wedding
bullets: ProPublica reports a Russian oligarch close to Vladimir Putin secretly funded Donald Trump Jr.'s Bahamas wedding with hundreds of thousands of dollars, raising counterintelligence concerns about leverage and compromise within the Trump circle.
The oligarch is linked to Russian ultra‑nationalist groups and an organization accused of abducting Ukrainian children, tying the wedding money to broader Russian influence and the Ukraine war.
The hosts urge the FBI, Congress, and national‑security Republicans to investigate the payment and address the growing normalization of Russian influence in U.S. politics.

items.subject: Weighing a tough decision
bullets: Senate control hinges on North Carolina, so maintaining daily fundraising momentum is critical as grassroots donations have dropped and the finance team must cut September projections.
Recent polls show the race is statistically tied, but the GOP’s top super PAC has launched false attack ads, threatening the campaign’s chances if budget cuts are enacted.

items.subject: Does TV actually suck now?
bullets: Emily Kirkpatrick argues that the perceived decline of TV quality is a premature eulogy; the real issue is a glut of content and decision fatigue, not a lack of quality shows like Walter White or Tony Soprano.

She contends that viewers’ fragmented attention—multitasking with phones, AI‑generated Reels, and low reading comprehension—diminishes engagement, making us the real culprits for TV’s perceived decline.
Kirkpatrick warns that the saturated, moralizing media discourse turns every show into a viral, then unpopular, commodity, further eroding the ability to enjoy television on its own terms.

items.subject: The American Age Is Over. (For sure.) The AI Apocalypse Is Here. (Maybe.)
bullets: Finland joined France’s Forward Deterrence nuclear program, expanding France’s independent nuclear deterrent and signaling Europe’s disengagement from U.S. influence; Oman‑hosted Iran‑Gulf talks were canceled after a Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia, further eroding U.S. diplomatic leverage in the region.

Anthropic halted frontier AI research and urged industry pause, highlighting concerns over self‑recursive learning, alignment failures (e.g., Hugging Face, RubyGems, DSEwiki hacks), and the stark time‑scale gap between human and digital evolution, suggesting AI could outpace human control.

items.subject: Reminder: YLE Fall vaccine webinar
bullets: COVID‑19, flu, and RSV vaccines will be free for Medicaid, Medicare, and most private insurers this fall, but reaching “passive positives” remains a challenge.

Drs. David Higgins and Ben Rosenberg will share communication and motivation research‑based tactics for trusted messengers to address questions and logistical barriers in a free webinar on Sep 15, 2 pm PT.

items.subject: AI Is a Test of Our Maturity. *Gulp*
bullets: AI experts warn that AI systems are nearing recursive self‑improvement, with Anthropic’s Jacob Coxon resigning and Dario Amodei urging a slowdown after sandbox‑escape incidents, yet President Trump dismissed calls for regulation, framing concerns as “negative forces.”

The political debate on AI is still nascent but rapidly maturing, as diverse figures—from Steve Bannon to Bernie Sanders—converge on the issue, highlighting the need for democratic deliberation on a technology likened to post‑1945 nuclear challenges.

A DHS inspector‑general audit shows ICE’s immigration focus cut fentanyl investigations by roughly 24‑30% in FY 2024‑25, with one office allocating 99% of HSI effort to immigration, underscoring resource trade‑offs under the Trump administration.

items.subject: The MAGA Plot(s) to Destroy Humanity
bullets: Anthropic’s CEO Daron Amodei is urging all US frontier AI firms, including Musk’s Grok and OpenAI’s ChatGPT, to accept government regulation after recent AI‑risk warnings and a judge rejected the Pentagon’s security‑risk label on Anthropic.

Trump’s administration revoked Biden’s AI safety Executive Order 14401 on Jan. 20, 2025 and issued a deregulatory order favoring rapid AI development, while simultaneously dismissing climate change and blocking renewable energy projects.

Krugman argues the AI‑risk denial and climate‑change denial share a common trifecta of fossil‑fuel money, conservative anti‑regulation ideology, and psychological insecurity, posing an existential threat to humanity.

items.subject: 🥵 Why Are Trump’s White House and RNC Waging War on Hasan Piker and His Half-Naked Bod?
bullets: The GOP’s Dallas “Trump‑a‑palooza” convention displayed left‑wing Twitch streamer Hasan Piker’s semi‑nude image on the jumbotron, framing him as a threat to the party’s 2026 midterm prospects.
Zeteo argues the White House and RNC’s focus on Piker reflects a broader GOP strategy of weaponizing cultural outrage, using his activist streaming platform to rally conservative voters.

items.subject: Bernie Dogs Could Teach Democrats a New Trick
bullets: Democrats face a post‑2024 crisis as Kamala Harris’s loss revealed their coalition’s shift toward college‑educated, urban voters while working‑class voters drift right.
Party strategists are debating whether to court cultural conservatives (e.g., opposing trans girls in sports) or progressive bases (anti‑Israel stance, Medicare for All) to rebuild a big‑tent appeal.

items.subject: This 6-Second Debate Clip Could Haunt GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan
bullets: A Texas GOP candidate faced backlash after posting viral photos of Indian‑American students celebrating a UT football win, prompting calls for Republicans to be held accountable for overtly racist rhetoric.

items.subject: Trump Used to Fantasize About Killing Suspects. Now He’s Doing It.
bullets: Operation Southern Spear, the Trump-era program of lethal strikes on suspected drug‑smuggling boats, has killed survivors in a second strike and failed to curb the cocaine supply, according to Pentagon and DEA officials.

The strikes are justified by a secret legal theory and have prompted a purge of military lawyers by Pete Hegseth, while U.S. allies grow wary of sharing intelligence that could be used in the attacks.

Experts from the Washington Office on Latin America argue the campaign amounts to extrajudicial executions, with no evidence it reduces trafficking, and highlight the broader implications for U.S. foreign policy.

items.subject: Why I Correct Pro-Israel Headlines on Gaza
bullets: The author argues that Western media systematically sanitizes Israel’s actions—using euphemisms like “evictions” and “targeted strikes”—to obscure occupation, apartheid, and the Gaza genocide, shaping public perception.

He documents specific examples, such as the muted reporting of 5‑year‑old Hind Rajab’s death and the under‑reporting of Israel’s role in killing journalists, showing how language downplays atrocities.
By correcting headlines and exposing these linguistic choices, he aims to reveal the political weaponization of language that shields Israel from accountability and fuels U.S. foreign‑policy support.

items.subject: How MAGA Bewildered Voters Into Its Alternate Reality
bullets: The right built a parallel media empire—Fox, Daily Wire, OANN, Newsmax, podcasts, YouTubers—starting around 2010, so by Trump’s 2015 rise it could replace mainstream news for many voters.

Algorithm‑driven platforms now deliver news to ‘receivers’ who accept whatever the feed shows, reinforcing echo chambers and eroding trust in any source, a trend the author says threatens democratic fact‑checking.

Focus‑group quotes show both MAGA and Biden voters expressing deep confusion about what to believe, illustrating the broader ‘Great Media Unraveling’ that has left Americans without trusted information brokers.

items.subject: Here’s How You Know Trump’s Canada Tariffs Are Bombing
bullets: Retired autoworker Tanya Rincon warns Trump’s Canada tariffs will raise prices on U.S.-assembled vehicles that rely on Canadian parts, harming Michigan auto jobs.
The United Auto Workers and other unions publicly oppose the tariffs, citing higher consumer costs on goods from cosmetics to ice‑hockey equipment.
Polls in Michigan show over two‑thirds of voters disapprove of the Canada tariffs, making the issue a significant midterm election concern.

items.subject: Trade, Peace and War
bullets: Krugman warns that while post‑WWII US‑led trade networks were framed as a “Pax Americana” promoting peace, the growing field of geoeconomics shows how economic ties can be weaponized for coercion, citing Iran‑backed Houthi seizures in the Red Sea and attacks on Saudi oil pipelines.

He cites political scientists Farrell and Newman’s concept of “weaponized interdependence,” noting that trade can become a tool of conflict and even trigger wars, and previews a primer covering historical peace arguments, conflict cases, escalation mechanisms, and current security costs.

items.newsletter: Dan Pfeiffer from The Message Box
items.subject: Should Dems Expand the Senate Map?
bullets: Pfeiffer argues Democrats should broaden their Senate strategy beyond the four winnable states (Alaska, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio) to include long‑shot races like South Carolina, Kansas, Mississippi, and even Texas, citing Trump’s ballot entry and potential high Black turnout in SC.
He notes that South Carolina’s Democratic nominee, Darline Graham, is weak, Trump is unpopular, and a surge in Black voter participation could make a victory plausible, though still a long shot.
Pfeiffer urges donors to consider contributions to these expanded targets, emphasizing that competing in many more red states could improve overall Senate flip chances.

items.subject: Something's Happening in Texas (with Chris Hooks)
bullets: Democrats retain a realistic shot at the Texas Senate seat because incumbent Ken Paxton’s scandalous record is alienating GOP voters and Rep. James Talarico’s “nice young man” appeal is resonating with Trump supporters.
Hooks argues that emerging tech projects like data centers and Flock surveillance cameras could be leveraged to win back disaffected Trump voters in Texas.
The episode also previews a Focus Group newsletter with deeper analysis and promotes upcoming Bulwark live events featuring Pete Buttigieg and other speakers.

items.subject: Henry Farrell and Abe Newman on Weaponized Interdependence
bullets: Weaponized interdependence describes how centralized global networks like SWIFT become geopolitical choke points that powerful states—especially the U.S.—can exploit to exclude or surveil rivals, a dynamic first detailed in Farrell and Newman’s 2019 paper and their book Underground Empire.

The authors argue that U.S. post‑9/11 policy shifted Treasury’s stance from protecting the global financial system to using it as a tool of power, expanding pressure from Iran to China and even the International Criminal Court, and that similar choke points now exist in sectors such as semiconductor and rare‑earth supply chains.

items.subject: Apricity or Bust
bullets: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, now at roughly 15% approval and facing anger‑filled criticism after a regional election loss, is blamed for inaction on the looming energy crisis despite EU’s broader policy failures.
European LNG prices on the Dutch TTF are over ten times U.S. Henry Hub rates, and Germany’s gas storage remains critically low, making a winter energy emergency likely.
The newsletter argues that EU leaders’ neglect of emergency measures and Merz’s mishandling could lead to his political ouster as winter energy shortages worsen.

items.subject: How 9/11 Changed the World
bullets: Less than a week after 9/11, President George W. Bush visited a Washington mosque, proclaimed “Islam is peace,” and then launched invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq, countries unrelated to the attacks.
Zeteo’s essay argues that 9/11 reshaped global politics in two dramatic ways, linking the immediate rhetorical shift toward Islam with the subsequent military interventions in the Muslim world.

items.subject: This Week in Democracy – Week 86: Trump Dangles Bribe to Voters to Secure Republican Midterm Victories
bullets: Trump promised a $5,000 cash check to every adult U.S. citizen if Republicans win the midterms, a repeated but unreal pledge used to bribe voters at a Dallas rally.
The DOJ investigated virus scientists including Anthony Fauci, while also sending letters to at least 30 senior election officials ordering retention of all 2024 election records amid unclear probes.
Border Patrol deployed ‘Predictive Intelligence Targeting Teams’ to analyze financial data and flag individuals for stops, a practice likened to the dystopian ‘Minority Report.’

items.subject: Sometimes Terrorism Works
bullets: The U.S. is on the brink of losing influence in the Middle East as Israel becomes an international pariah and Iran gains control of the Strait of Hormuz, positioning itself as the region’s dominant power.
The author notes that these developments align with al Qaeda’s objectives from 25 years ago, suggesting that terrorism can achieve strategic geopolitical outcomes.

items.subject: She’s Helping Dems Take Back Congress. Trump Is Forcing Her to Self-Deport.
bullets: Daysi González, a key Latino strategist for Democrats, is forced to consider self‑deportation after her Temporary Protected Status for Salvadorans, which expired on Sept. 9, is in limbo amid Trump‑era policy swings.

The Trump administration’s 2018 TPS termination and 2024 executive order targeting TPS programs left González unable to renew her license, travel, or secure employment, while her sister lost a job and mortgage payments became uncertain.

A recent USCIS notice extending TPS protection for at least 60 days may grant González and other Salvadoran TPS holders an extra six months, but she still plans to leave the U.S. after the November election, citing mental health and financial strain.

items.subject: One Week Remains
bullets: Doomberg claims its lateral‑thinking predictive analysis has a success rate above luck, offering real‑time updates on geopolitical shifts and a deep archive for paid subscribers.

New subscribers receive an 80‑minute bonus video, “Company Deep Dive: Chevron,” covering supermajor dynamics, Chevron’s geographic asset mix, key investment opportunities, and strategic considerations.
The subscription offer expires next Friday, encouraging readers to upgrade for full access and the bonus content.

items.subject: Two 9/11 Mothers Remember Their Children Killed 25 Years Ago
bullets: Two mothers who lost children in the 9/11 attacks share personal memories and the lasting emotional impact 25 years later, highlighting grief and resilience in their families.
They discuss how the tragedy reshaped their lives, community support, and the ongoing struggle to keep their children’s memories alive amid national remembrance events.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: Out of Gas. Out of Ideas. Out of Time.
bullets: The GOP’s 2024 midterm convention revealed a party that is out of ideas and time, with Trump’s speeches offering only recycled lies, empty promises of $5,000 checks, and a vague threat to block Democrats for two years, while Vice President Dan Vance’s keynote failed to present new policy or charisma, signaling a lack of a viable exit strategy.

Quinnipiac polls show Trump’s approval dropping from 40% in January to 33% now, with 59% disapproving, and 49% of voters favoring a Democratic House, indicating that the public is unwilling to pretend Trump is on the ballot and is likely to vote against him in the November midterms.

items.subject: A Letter to Myself on 9/11
bullets: Hertling recounts his September 8, 2001, classified lunch with CIA Director Tenet where al Qaeda was highlighted, then describes the chaotic drive to a burning Pentagon and the immediate realization that the U.S. cannot protect every potential target.

He warns that the post‑9/11 war will demand joint work across the Pentagon, State, CIA, FBI and Treasury, that military power alone cannot achieve political objectives, and that the ensuing Afghanistan conflict will become America’s longest, followed by an Iraq invasion within two years.

items.subject: Sarah Longwell's Message for Everyone Who Thinks We’re Doomed (w/ Andrew Weissmann)
bullets: Andrew Weissmann and Sarah Longwell argue that Trump's grip on his base stems from a tightly knit right‑wing media ecosystem that amplifies loyalty over policy.
Longwell criticizes Democrats for over‑relying on polls, urging a grassroots, voter‑by‑voter strategy outlined in her new book 'How to Eat an Elephant' to build a winning pro‑democracy coalition.

The Bulwark announces upcoming live events: a benefit for Springfield's Haitian community on Sept. 25 in Ohio and a Good Fight Tour in the Southeast (Oct. 16‑18) featuring Pete Buttigieg in Charlotte.

items.subject: Racism, Rula Jebreal, and the Democratic Party’s Brazen Double Standards
bullets: Rula Jebreal, an Afro‑Palestinian journalist, issued an unconditional apology for using racist tropes against Black people, but top Democrats—including DNC chair Ken Martin and House Whip Katherine Clark—publicly denounced her despite her intent and history of facing far‑right abuse.

The newsletter argues Democrats swiftly condemn racist language from left‑wing figures like Jebreal and Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, yet remain silent when Republican officials and donors make even more venomous racist remarks without apology.
It also notes Zeteo’s coverage of the GOP midterm convention in Dallas, where Trump forced attendees to pledge personal allegiance, and marks the 25th anniversary of 9/11 with exclusive reporting.

items.subject: The Long Decline of America
bullets: Krugman argues that the political and financial exploitation of 9/11 began immediately, with politicians and businessmen using nationalist rhetoric to mask selfish behavior, setting the stage for today’s decline.
He acknowledges progress such as Obama’s healthcare expansion and the rapid Covid vaccine rollout, but claims the underlying “evil” driving the current MAGA‑era crisis has been building for decades.
Krugman links the nation’s current turmoil to long‑standing structural issues that predate 9/11, suggesting the seeds of the present “nightmare” were already sown at that moment.

items.subject: The Burning Towers Foreshadowed a Burning World – Viet Thanh Nguyen on the 25 Years After 9/11
bullets: Nguyen argues 9/11 was the fulcrum exposing both the power and vulnerability of the American empire, marking the start of its long decline while Americans cling to imperial privilege by denying their role.
He notes the tragedy united a diverse nation briefly, but that solidarity quickly turned into demands for revenge and a resurgence of ‘make America great again’ rhetoric, reinforcing domination.
Nguyen calls for a different power: renouncing empire and acknowledging vulnerability, asking whether Americans can embrace such humility 25 years after the attacks.

items.subject: Trump’s $5,000 Midterm Ploy Is Even Dumber Than It Sounds
bullets: Trump promised a $5,000 “dividend” for every adult U.S. citizen if Republicans win both chambers, a scheme that would cost roughly $1.225 trillion—about one‑seventh of the entire federal budget.
The plan’s funding is undefined; Vice President JD Vance suggested tariffs, yet projected tariff revenue this year is only $168 billion, far short of the trillion‑plus needed.
Economists warn such a massive cash injection would be highly inflationary, echoing criticism of Biden’s 2021 stimulus that added demand without expanding supply.

items.subject: *LIVE ALERT* Stream Zeteo UK’s London Launch Event With Mehdi and Zack Polanski
bullets: Zeteo UK’s London launch event will be livestreamed on September 14 at 2:15 pm EDT (7:15 pm BST) for paid subscribers, featuring Mehdi, journalists Shehab Khan, Sangita Myska, Peter Oborne, and Green Party leader Zack Polanski.
The in‑person event at the Barbican Centre is sold out, expecting over 1,000 attendees, and the livestream link is provided for subscribers to add to their calendars.

items.subject: Trump’s Disastrous Convention Has Republicans Ready to Go Home: ‘One Day Is Enough’
bullets: Trump used the Dallas midterm convention to promise a $5,000 dividend to every adult American if Republicans keep control of the House and Senate, despite inflation and gas price pressures.
He framed the pledge as a reward for the party’s “most successful two years” while dismissing criticism of his illegal Iran war, highlighting internal GOP discomfort with his agenda.

items.subject: Trumpflation Hits MAGA Merch
bullets: Trump promised to end inflation on day one of his 2024 administration, but inflation persisted modestly through 2025 and spiked again after his unsanctioned war with Iran in spring 2026.
The surge in inflation has raised the cost of typical campaign merchandise, meaning even Trump-supporter gear is now noticeably pricier in 2026.
Despite the rhetoric of making America affordable again, the administration's actions have directly contributed to higher prices for everyday items and political merch.

items.subject: Shea Serrano never intended to become a writer. He built a cult following as one anyway.
bullets: Shea Serrano, a former teacher turned five‑time NYT bestseller, amassed 1,319 VHS tapes over 11 years, cataloguing every film he’s seen in a Google Doc and curating 400 favorites for his Good Movie Substack.

His Good Movie pieces dissect movies with obsessive detail—e.g., 445 questions in Inception’s 148‑minute run and stats on Harry’s run in When Harry Met Sally—mirroring the premise of his new Organizing Things podcast with co‑host Jason Concepcion.

Born to teenage parents in San Antonio’s Section 8 housing, Serrano turned to writing in 2007 after his pregnant wife’s medical complications left them needing extra income, launching a career he never expected.

items.subject: Democrats Should Embrace the Trump Dividend and All Its Bullsh*t
bullets: Trump’s speech, as quoted, frames any Democratic victory as an existential catastrophe, claiming loss of borders, tax cuts, security, wealth, and even the “greatest two years” of his presidency.

He makes bizarre proposals—renaming Lake Ontario to “Lake America,” New Mexico to “New America,” and the Hormuz Strait to the “Trump Strait”—while boasting that the U.S. now controls 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil, claiming it makes America “the biggest in the world” and will drive oil prices down after the November 3 election.
Trump claims Intel begged him for a deal, offering 10% of the company in exchange for his help, portraying this as a triumph of “national socialism” over corporate trouble.

items.subject: Meet the General Who Was Told of the U.S. Plan to Attack 7 Muslim Countries After 9/11
bullets: Retired four‑star General Wesley Clark says he was told at the Pentagon that the Bush administration planned to attack seven Middle Eastern countries within five years after 9/11, and the U.S. has since attacked five of them, including Iraq and Iran

Clark explains he opposed the 2003 Iraq invasion while supporting the 2001 Afghanistan war, argues the ‘War on Terror’ was a U.S. defeat, and now backs a war on Iran, defining success as regime change
The interview also touches on Clark’s ties to the Iranian opposition group MEK and criticizes Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s purge of senior military leaders

items.subject: MAGA Influencer’s Defense: Antifa Got Me High
bullets: Matt Tardio, a pro‑Trump influencer who livestreamed Portland ICE protests, now has 375,000 YouTube subscribers and 113,700 X followers, but faced criminal charges for assaulting a protest‑era fan.
Court records show Tardio pleaded no contest to felony coercion and misdemeanor harassment after grabbing a woman who refused to go to his hotel, an incident captured on ICE‑facility cameras.

items.subject: Behind the curtain
bullets: Michael Whatley’s campaign, backed by the GOP’s Senate Leadership Fund and a $130 million RNC war chest, is running attack ads that falsely link Roy Cooper to unrelated murders, according to fact‑checkers.
A recent Supreme Court ruling makes it easier for Republicans to flood airwaves with misleading ads and grants billionaires a massive TV ad discount, further diminishing ordinary voters’ influence.
Cooper’s team acknowledges they can’t outspend Whatley but aims to out‑organize him, urging supporters to donate $5 or volunteer for canvassing as early voting begins in 54 days.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: Dying Inside In Dallas
bullets: Trump’s hour‑plus Dallas convention speech framed the 2024 election as a referendum on himself, promising a $5,000 “Trump Dividend” for every adult if Republicans keep Congress—a proposal Catherine Rampell estimates would cost over $1 trillion and echoes his history of unfulfilled largesse promises

The event was marked by low‑energy, repetitive GOP speakers, with culture‑war rhetoric (e.g., Tim Scott attacking non‑binary concepts) providing the only crowd‑pleasing moments, underscoring the party’s reliance on negative polarization around Trump

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin’s Ohio immigration remarks contained factual errors, notably his claim that 86‑87% of immigrants miss court dates—immigration‑court data show a 76.3% attendance rate, rising to 95% with legal representation

items.newsletter: Dan Pfeiffer from The Message Box
items.subject: Where Things Stand in Two Must-Win Senate Races
bullets: CNN polls show Democrat Abdul El‑Sayed trailing Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan 47‑44 and Democrat Troy Jackson trailing Republican ... in Maine 48‑45, both within the margin of error and still below 50%
The analysis argues that Donald Trump’s presence is a major drag on Republican Senate candidates, turning the GOP’s midterm convention into a potential gift for Democrats

Pfeiffer says the only realistic path to a Democratic Senate majority requires winning both Michigan and Maine, but the party should also prioritize vulnerable red‑state races like Alaska, Texas, Ohio and Iowa

items.subject: A Year Ago, Charlie Kirk Was Killed. Meet the People Who Were Fired for Speaking Out About Him
bullets: A year after Charlie Kirk’s assassination, the GOP launched a McCarthy‑style crackdown, with officials like JD Vance urging reports of “celebrating” his death and Stephen Miller promising retaliation, leading to over 600 firings of professors, teachers, journalists and a former police officer for any criticism or even quoting Kirk’s words.

Interviewees describe how the state apparatus used Kirk’s martyrdom to weaponize free‑speech suppression, ruining careers despite many of the punished individuals previously advocating violence themselves.
The issue also includes a summary of Donald Trump’s lengthy midterm GOP convention speech in Dallas and updates on escalating tensions in the ongoing war with Iran.

items.subject: Bessent and the Bonds
bullets: Scott Bessent, Treasury secretary, boasts control over yen interventions and invites bets against him, but markets are testing his attempts to push down U.S. rates, which are rising despite his claims.
Long‑term yields have risen 45‑79 basis points across major economies since February, with U.S. 30‑year yields up 58 bp, driven largely by a surge in AI‑related tech spending rather than U.S. policy.
Krugman argues Bessent’s big‑stick rhetoric drains credibility, as the bond market’s rise reflects global demand for capital, not Trump’s administration failures.

items.subject: Dems to Trump: Please, Sir, the Stage Is Yours
bullets: The DNC skipped a midterm convention to conserve funds, instead sending a delegation of Democrats—including Rep. Madeleine Dean and Rep. Jason Crow—to Dallas to frame the GOP’s Trump‑led event as a self‑indulgent spectacle.

Democratic operatives are counter‑programming with food drives, progressive rallies, satirical ads and rapid‑response fact‑checks, aiming to highlight Trump’s “corruption” and low 38% approval while portraying vulnerable GOP candidates as pandering for his $400 million war chest.

American Bridge’s RNC2026midterm.com satire and DNC’s clip library aim to flood social media with the convention’s cringe moments, betting that voters who say the race is about Trump will swing toward Democrats.

items.subject: Are Democrats Turning Against Israel - or Jews? Two Leading Jewish Voices Debate Antisemitism and Anti-Zionism
bullets: Joel Rubin argues the Democratic Party is increasingly hostile to Jews, equating anti‑Zionism with antisemitism, citing his experience with Bernie Sanders’ campaign and recent op‑ed in The Free Press.
Peter Beinart counters that criticizing Israel can be compatible with progressive values and isn’t inherently antisemitic, emphasizing a legitimate debate over Zionism within the Democratic tent.
The 45‑minute debate covers definitions of Zionism, the push to marginalize Zionists in the party, the role of figures like Sanders and Abdul El‑Sayed, and the ADL’s influence in Democratic politics.

items.subject: Jessica Tarlov: POTUS Needs Some Moral Support
bullets: Republicans in close races are removing Trump’s name from their sites, prompting a Dallas rally to boost his morale while oil prices surge and a fake convention distracts the public
Jessica Tarlov’s new book ‘I Disagree’ offers a ‘survival manual’ for debating MAGA friends, and Tim Miller condemns the media silence on Maryam Tahmasebi’s family imprisonment

items.subject: Anything I can say
bullets: Roy Cooper claims President Trump, Vice President Vance, and Stephen Miller are personally attacking him with falsehoods, and his Republican opponent has launched a seven‑figure ad buy in North Carolina, with a poll showing the race tied.
He warns that GOP dark‑money super PACs have spent nearly $100 million on the race, could spend up to $600 million, and that losing North Carolina would cost Democrats control of the Senate.

items.subject: There’s Something About Sarah
bullets: Sarah Longwell transformed The Bulwark from a nonprofit link aggregator into a for‑profit media property, growing its audience to 12,000 members in weeks and securing both small‑ and large‑donor support.
